questionText:
An element X of period 3 with atomic mass 27 amu carries 3 electrons in its valence shell.
Calculate its number of electrons, protons and neutrons if atom X loses all of its valence electrons.
sloText: Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in atoms and ions;
checkingHints: 1 mark for calculating correct number of protons (13 protons).
1 mark for calculating correct number of electrons after losing 3 valence electrons (10 electrons).
1 mark for calculating correct number of neutrons (27 - 13 = 14 neutrons).

rubric.description: Number of protons = 13 (derived from Period 3 with 3 valence electrons: Al, Z = 13).
Number of electrons in ion = 13 - 3 = 10 electrons.
Number of neutrons = Mass number (A) - Atomic number (Z) = 27 - 13 = 14 neutrons.

modelAnswer:
Identification of Element X:
- Period 3 element with 3 valence electrons is Aluminum (Al), having Atomic number (Z) = 13 and Mass number (A) = 27.

Calculations for the ion (Al3+ after losing all 3 valence electrons):
1. Number of protons = 13 (proton count is unchanged during chemical reactions).
2. Number of electrons = 13 - 3 = 10 electrons.
3. Number of neutrons = Atomic mass - Atomic number = 27 - 13 = 14 neutrons.

questionText:
Complete the given table by choosing the correct element for each property from the following list.
• Fluorine
• Sodium
• Sulphur
• Carbon
• Oxygen
• Helium

1. It produces a basic oxide on reaction with oxygen.
2. It is an unreactive, colourless gas.
3. It has an oxidation state of negative one.
sloText: Identify elements and periodic properties based on oxide nature, reactivity, and oxidation states;
checkingHints: 1 mark for identifying Sodium as the metal forming basic oxide.
1 mark for identifying Helium as the unreactive noble gas.
1 mark for identifying Fluorine as having an oxidation state of -1.

rubric.description: Property 1 (basic oxide): Sodium (forms Na2O, which dissolves in water to form NaOH).
Property 2 (unreactive, colourless gas): Helium (Group 18 noble gas).
Property 3 (oxidation state of -1): Fluorine (most electronegative element, exclusively -1 in compounds).

modelAnswer:
1. It produces a basic oxide on reaction with oxygen: Sodium (Na)
2. It is an unreactive, colourless gas: Helium (He)
3. It has an oxidation state of negative one: Fluorine (F)

questionText:
a. Describe the movement of particles in liquid state. (1 Mark)
b. If the liquid is exposed to cold temperatures, what will be the effect on the movement of particles? (1 Mark)
c. If the same number of particles of a gas and liquid are placed in a container at standard temperature and pressure, then why the volume of the gas is found to be greater than that of liquid? (1 Mark)
sloText: Explain the kinetic molecular theory of matter across states and phase changes;
checkingHints: 1 mark for describing particle motion in liquids (continuous random sliding/flowing past one another).
1 mark for stating that cold temperature reduces kinetic energy and slows down particle movement.
1 mark for explaining that gas particles have negligible intermolecular attraction and vast intermolecular spaces compared to liquids.

rubric.description: Part a: Particles in a liquid move randomly, sliding, rolling, and flowing past each other while remaining in continuous contact.
Part b: At cold temperatures, average kinetic energy decreases, causing particle velocity to slow down and particles to move closer together.
Part c: Gas particles possess very weak/negligible intermolecular forces and huge intermolecular spaces between them compared to the closely packed particles in a liquid.

modelAnswer:
a. In a liquid, particles are closely packed but can slide, roll, and flow freely over one another in continuous random motion.
b. When exposed to cold temperatures, the average kinetic energy of the particles decreases, causing their movement to slow down significantly as intermolecular attractions pull them closer together.
c. Gas particles have negligible intermolecular forces and are separated by extremely large intermolecular distances compared to liquid particles; therefore, the same number of gas particles spreads out to occupy a vastly larger volume.

questionText:
Give a reason why metals:
a. have high melting points. (1 Mark)
b. are good conductors of electricity. (1 Mark)
c. are malleable and ductile. (1 Mark)
d. are lustrous. (1 Mark)
sloText: Explain physical properties of metals in terms of metallic bonding and delocalised electrons;
checkingHints: 1 mark for relating high melting points to strong electrostatic attractions between cations and delocalised electrons.
1 mark for relating electrical conductivity to free mobile delocalised electrons.
1 mark for explaining malleability/ductility by the sliding of ion layers without breaking metallic bonding.
1 mark for explaining luster by the reflection/re-emission of light by mobile electrons.

rubric.description: High melting points: Strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons requires large amounts of energy to overcome.
Electrical conductivity: Free, mobile delocalised electrons are able to drift towards the positive terminal when a potential difference is applied.
Malleable and ductile: Layers of positive ions can slide past each other under stress without fracturing, as the sea of mobile electrons immediately adjusts to maintain bonding.
Lustrous: De-localised surface electrons absorb incident photons and re-emit/reflect light uniformly, producing a shiny metallic luster.

modelAnswer:
a. High melting points: Metals consist of a giant lattice with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between positive metal cations and the surrounding sea of delocalised electrons, requiring substantial thermal energy to break.
b. Electrical conductivity: Metals contain free mobile delocalised electrons that drift freely through the crystal lattice when an electric field is applied.
c. Malleability and ductility: When mechanical force is applied, layers of metal ions slide over each other without disrupting the non-directional metallic bond, as the delocalised electrons flow to cushion the sliding ions.
d. Lustrous: The free delocalised electrons on the metal's polished surface readily absorb and immediately re-emit (reflect) light of all visible wavelengths.

questionText:
A compound contains 24% carbon, 12% hydrogen and 64% oxygen by mass. The relative molecular mass of this compound is 50.057 g/mol.
i. Calculate the empirical formula of the given compound. (4 Marks)
ii. Determine its molecular formula. (2 Marks)
(Note: Atomic mass of C = 12 amu, H = 1 amu and O = 16 amu)
sloText: Calculate empirical and molecular formulas from percentage composition and molar mass;
checkingHints: 1 mark for calculating moles of each element (C = 24/12 = 2.0; H = 12/1 = 12.0; O = 64/16 = 4.0).
1 mark for finding simplest atomic ratio by dividing by the smallest mole value (2.0).
1 mark for deducing empirical formula as CH6O2.
1 mark for calculating empirical formula mass (12 + 6 + 32 = 50 g/mol).
1 mark for finding n = 50.057 / 50 ≈ 1.
1 mark for writing correct molecular formula as CH6O2.

rubric.description: Number of moles: Moles of C = 24/12 = 2.0; Moles of H = 12/1 = 12.0; Moles of O = 64/16 = 4.0.
Empirical formula is CH6O2 (4 marks total for part i).
Molecular formula = (CH6O2) * 1 = CH6O2 (2 marks for part ii).

modelAnswer:
i. Calculation of Empirical Formula:
1. Moles of each element in 100 g of compound:
   - Moles of Carbon (C) = 24 g / 12 g/mol = 2.0 mol
   - Moles of Hydrogen (H) = 12 g / 1 g/mol = 12.0 mol
   - Moles of Oxygen (O) = 64 g / 16 g/mol = 4.0 mol

2. Simplest atomic mole ratio (divide by 2.0):
   - C : 2.0 / 2.0 = 1
   - H : 12.0 / 2.0 = 6
   - O : 4.0 / 2.0 = 2

Empirical Formula = CH6O2

ii. Determination of Molecular Formula:
1. Empirical formula mass of CH6O2 = (1 * 12) + (6 * 1) + (2 * 16) = 12 + 6 + 32 = 50 g/mol
2. Scaling factor n = Molecular mass / Empirical mass = 50.057 / 50 = 1.001 ≈ 1
3. Molecular formula = n * (Empirical formula) = 1 * (CH6O2) = CH6O2

questionText:
The given graph represents the effect of temperature on the solubility of sodium sulphate.
With reference to this graph, answer the following questions.
i. Identify the approximate minimum and maximum solubility of Na2SO4. (2 Marks)
ii. Interpret the trend of solubility of Na2SO4 depicted in this graph. (2 Marks)
iii. By mentioning the guiding rule of solubility, describe any ONE factor that affects the solubility of any salt. (2 Marks)
sloText: Interpret solubility curves and describe factors affecting solubility;
checkingHints: 1 mark for minimum solubility (~5 g per 100 g H2O at 0 °C) and 1 mark for maximum solubility (~50 g per 100 g H2O at ~32.4 °C).
1 mark for noting sharp increase from 0 °C to ~32.4 °C, and 1 mark for noting the gradual decrease after ~32.4 °C.
1 mark for stating 'Like dissolves like' and 1 mark for explaining temperature effect or nature of solute/solvent.

rubric.description: Minimum solubility: ~4 to 5 g of Na2SO4 per 100 g of water (at 0 °C).
Maximum solubility: ~50 g of Na2SO4 per 100 g of water (at around 32.4 °C).

Trend interpretation: Solubility increases steeply with temperature up to approximately 32.4 °C (due to dissolution of decahydrate Na2SO4·10H2O). Above 32.4 °C, the curve changes slope and solubility decreases slightly with increasing temperature (anhydrous Na2SO4).
Guiding rule: 'Like dissolves like' (polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents).
Factor: Temperature (for endothermic dissolution, solubility increases with temperature; for exothermic, it decreases) OR Solute-solvent intermolecular interactions.

modelAnswer:
i. Solubility Extremes from Graph:
- Approximate minimum solubility: ~5 g per 100 g of H2O (at 0 °C).
- Approximate maximum solubility: ~50 g per 100 g of H2O (at approximately 32.4 °C).

ii. Interpretation of Solubility Trend:
- From 0 °C to approximately 32.4 °C, the solubility of sodium sulphate increases sharply with temperature as the decahydrate form (Na2SO4·10H2O) dissolves endothermically.
- Above 32.4 °C, the compound transitions into its anhydrous form (Na2SO4), and its dissolution becomes exothermic, causing solubility to gradually decrease with further increase in temperature.

iii. Guiding Rule & Factor:
- Guiding rule of solubility: 'Like dissolves like' — polar ionic solutes dissolve readily in polar solvents like water, while non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.
- Factor affecting solubility (Temperature): In salts where dissolution is endothermic (heat absorbed, ΔH > 0), increasing temperature supplies thermal energy, shifting equilibrium forward and increasing solubility. In exothermic dissolution (heat released, ΔH < 0), increasing temperature suppresses solubility.

questionText:
Given are the diagrams of two different molecules, P and Q.
The following table provides information about each element of these molecules.
Element X: Group 5, Period 2
Element Y: Group 1, Period 1
Element Z: Group 7, Period 3

Using the given information, answer the following questions.
i. Identify the molecules, P and Q. (2 Marks)
ii. If molecules P and Q combine chemically, then
   I. draw a dot and cross structure to represent the newly formed compound. (1 Mark)
   II. name the bond that forms between the two molecules and write any TWO specific characteristics of compounds having this bond. (3 Marks)
sloText: Describe coordinate covalent bonding and properties of coordinate compounds;
checkingHints: 1 mark for identifying Molecule P as Ammonia (NH3) and 1 mark for Molecule Q as Hydrogen chloride (HCl).
1 mark for drawing/describing dot-and-cross structure of ammonium chloride [NH4]+ [Cl]-.
1 mark for naming Coordinate covalent (dative) bond, and 2 marks for stating two valid characteristics of coordinate compounds.

rubric.description: Molecule P: Ammonia (NH3) [Element X = Nitrogen, Element Y = Hydrogen].
Molecule Q: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) [Element Y = Hydrogen, Element Z = Chlorine].
Structure: Dot and cross representation of [NH4]+ and Cl- (lone pair on N donated to H+ forming NH4+).
Bond name: Coordinate covalent bond (dative covalent bond).
Characteristics: 1. Higher melting/boiling points than simple covalent molecules, 2. Polar nature dissolving in polar solvents, 3. Directional bonding nature.

modelAnswer:
i. Identification of Molecules:
- Element X (Group 5, Period 2) is Nitrogen (N).
- Element Y (Group 1, Period 1) is Hydrogen (H).
- Element Z (Group 7, Period 3) is Chlorine (Cl).
- Molecule P = NH3 (Ammonia)
- Molecule Q = HCl (Hydrogen chloride)

ii. Chemical Combination:
I. Dot and Cross Structure of Ammonium Chloride (NH4Cl):
   Ammonia donates its unshared pair of electrons (lone pair on N) to the proton (H+) from HCl, forming the ammonium ion [NH4]+ and leaving the chloride ion [Cl]-:
   [ H : N(H)(H) -> H ]+ [ :Cl: ]-
   (Nitrogen shares its two non-bonding electrons with H+ through coordinate covalent bonding).

II. Bond Name and Characteristics:
- Name of bond: Coordinate Covalent (Dative) Bond.
- Characteristics of compounds with coordinate bonds:
  1. Moderate to high melting and boiling points compared to purely covalent compounds due to semi-polar nature.
  2. Soluble in polar solvents (like water) and insoluble in non-polar organic solvents.
  3. Shows directional characteristics in the donor-acceptor linkage.

questionText:
Given below is the image of a zinc-carbon battery.
i. What is the anode and cathode made up of in the given dry cell battery? (2 Marks)
ii. How does the zinc-carbon battery work? Support your answer using balanced chemical equations for the reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode. (4 Marks)
sloText: Describe the construction, working, and chemical reactions of a dry cell (zinc-carbon battery);
checkingHints: 1 mark for identifying Anode as Zinc metal container/casing.
1 mark for identifying Cathode as Carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by MnO2.
2 marks for clear explanation of battery working mechanism (oxidation of zinc, electron flow, reduction of MnO2).
1 mark for balanced anode half-reaction: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-.
1 mark for balanced cathode half-reaction: 2MnO2 + 2NH4+ + 2e- -> Mn2O3 + 2NH3 + H2O.

rubric.description: Anode composition: Outer Zinc (Zn) can/container.
Cathode composition: Central Carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by manganese dioxide (MnO2) and carbon powder.

Working mechanism: Zinc oxidizes at the anode releasing electrons; electrons pass through the external circuit to provide power; at the cathode, manganese dioxide is reduced in the presence of NH4+ ions from the ammonium chloride electrolyte paste.
Anode reaction: Zn(s) -> Zn2+(aq) + 2e- (Oxidation).
Cathode reaction: 2MnO2(s) + 2NH4+(aq) + 2e- -> Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(aq) + H2O(l) (Reduction).

modelAnswer:
i. Composition of Electrodes in Dry Cell:
- Anode (-): Outer zinc metal container / casing.
- Cathode (+): Central graphite (carbon) rod packed in a mixture of manganese dioxide (MnO2) and powdered carbon.

ii. Working of Zinc-Carbon Battery:
1. At the anode (oxidation half-reaction):
   Zinc atoms in the container lose two electrons each to form zinc ions (Zn2+), undergoing oxidation:
   Zn(s) -> Zn2+(aq) + 2e-

2. External electron flow:
   The liberated electrons flow from the zinc anode through the external electrical circuit to the carbon cathode, generating an electric potential of approximately 1.5 V.

3. At the cathode (reduction half-reaction):
   Electrons arriving at the carbon rod reduce manganese dioxide (MnO2) from oxidation state +4 to +3 in the presence of ammonium ions from the wet electrolyte paste (NH4Cl and ZnCl2):
   2MnO2(s) + 2NH4+(aq) + 2e- -> Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(aq) + H2O(l)

4. Overall Cell Reaction:
   Zn(s) + 2MnO2(s) + 2NH4Cl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(aq) + H2O(l)
